# Chapter 6 — Adopting Without Replacing

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
Nothing in this series asks an enterprise to replace a platform. The closing chapter lays out the adoption sequence — the same assess-derive-stamp-watch loop the Microsoft estate proved, repeated per profile — and then does what closing chapters too rarely do: states precisely which pieces are shipped, governed canon today and which are specified but awaiting their transports, so that a reader can plan against the actual state of the substrate rather than the trajectory of the prose.
:::

## The Loop Is Already Proven

The Microsoft estate did the substrate a favor beyond hosting it first: it established the adoption loop that every subsequent platform reuses. The loop has four movements. *Assess* reads the platform's native objects — directory entries, instances, virtual machines — through the profile's read side, surfacing what organizational truth the platform already holds, however informally. *Derive* translates those native attributes into codebook values through a mapping that is deliberately operator-tunable: the default ships in code, the tenant override travels as configuration, and the distinction between canon and configuration stays sharp. *Stamp* writes the derived facets back through the profile's locators, dry-run by default, applying only when told to. *Watch* hands the stamped surface to the drift engine, which from that moment treats the platform as part of the reconciled estate.

Nothing in the loop is Microsoft-specific, which is the point. Extending governance to a new platform is not a migration project with a war room; it is the same four movements against a different profile. The platforms already running stay running. The directories already authoritative stay authoritative — the loop reads them, derives from them, and stamps alongside them. Adoption is additive by construction, because every movement is either read-only or dry-run until an operator says otherwise.

## Sequencing the Estate

Which platform goes first is a judgment call, but the profiles themselves suggest the order. Okta is the gentlest on-ramp: a pure identity plane, native room for every facet, no overflow rule to reason about — an enterprise federating through Okta can prove the loop end-to-end there with the least surface area at risk. Generic LDAP follows naturally where Red Hat IdM or another directory anchors the on-premises estate, with the one governed decision of schema-extension versus reserved-attribute mode made up front. The cloud platforms come next, identity plane before workload plane, because the identity bindings fit without constraint while the workload bindings deserve a deliberate look at the tag budget and the overflow ordering. VMware lands last not because it is hardest but because it is widest — three planes adopted in the same order, identity, then workload, then enforcement, with the NSX bindings arriving only when the segmentation program is ready to consume them.

Threaded through the sequence is one rule that keeps the estate coherent: the codebook never forks. A platform joining the substrate adopts the enumerations the estate already governs; it does not negotiate its own dialect. The profiles vary, the constraints vary, the overflow orderings vary — the meaning does not.

## What Ships, What Waits

A series like this one owes its reader a precise inventory, because prose has a way of narrating futures in the present tense. As of this writing, the inventory is as follows.

Shipped and governed: the decision record itself — ADR-098 — and the full specification, UIAO_193, including the Zero Trust projection this series' fifth chapter narrates. Shipped and enforced: the binding-profile JSON Schema; the six executable profiles — the Microsoft reference, AWS, Google Cloud, Okta, LDAP, VMware — as validated canon; and the loader that refuses, in continuous integration, any profile that binds an unknown facet, collides a locator, breaks an overflow ordering, or claims a boundary outside Moderate and Commercial. The Microsoft estate's transports — Graph for the directory, Azure Resource Manager for the Arc device plane — are shipped and in production use, which is why the reference profile is marked *reference* while the other five carry the status *proposed*.

Specified and pending: the per-platform transports that make the other five profiles operational — the mapping and write modules for Okta, LDAP, the clouds, and the VMware surfaces — and, behind them, the enforcement-projection compiler that turns facet predicates into NSX groups, dynamic address groups, and their peers. The architecture those components slot into is fixed; the contract they must satisfy is validated canon; the loop they will run is proven on the estate that has run it for chapters of the companion series. What waits is the connectors, and connectors against a fixed contract are engineering, not research.

A reader weighing the substrate should hold both halves of that inventory at once. The half that is hardest to get right — the model, the governance, the contract, the enforcement of the contract — exists and is exercised by machinery on every commit. The half that remains is the half the industry knows how to build.

## The Closing Argument

The OrgPath series ended on a positioning claim: that the substrate is the layer the governance platforms compose against rather than compete with. This series ends one step further out. The substrate is also the layer the *platforms* compose against — Microsoft and Okta and the clouds and the virtualization estate — because organizational truth is the one thing in an enterprise that should not be multi-sourced. Fifteen facets, one codebook, a typed drift engine, and now a contract that lets the truth live wherever the enterprise actually is.

Governance beyond Entra and Azure is not a roadmap item. It is a profile away.
